newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Debt Office sees '97 PSBR at 25-35 bln skr.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Debt Office sees '97 PSBR at 25-35 bln skr.

text.p: Sweden's National Debt Office said on Thursday it forecast the country's 1997 state borrowing requirement between 25 and 35 billion crowns.
This compares to the current estimate for 1996 of 20 to 30 billion crowns, the Debt Office said in a statement.
It said the 1997 forecast included non-recurring revenue of 25 billion crowns from out of sales of state-owned assets, which was consistent with the measures outlined in the Swedish budget.
However, strong economic fundamentals meant that the underlying primary balance also continued to improve the debt office said.
The office said the macro-economic picture outlined by the Swedish National Economic Research Institute (KI) in an August report had been used as the basis for the forecast.
This report said tax payments would continue to rise as the underlying economy picked up.
The debt office said the reduction in the 1996 borrwing requirement had to a large extent been due to a number of non-recurring effects.
These included the transfer of assets of the Nuclear Waste Fund to the Debt Office's current account and change in the VAT payment and reporting periods.
Even so, non-recurring revenue in 1997 will be some 20-25 billion crowns less than in 1996.
The Debt Office said the state borrowing need was reduced by the early redemption of loans by a number of state enterprises.
"The Swedish National Debt Office's net lending is expected to decline further in 1997 although at a far slower pace," it said.
Interest on the government debt is estimated to be about the same as in 1996.
However, borrowing in the form of index-linked treasury bonds rose sharply in 1996 with the greater part of interest not paid until the bonds mature.

Periodisation of these and other interest payments with the object of estimating the cost of interest on the central government debt indicates these costs will exceed the interest actually payable in 1997 by some five billion crowns.
Interest payments are included in the borrowing requirement.

"The fact that the borrowing requirement will only increase marginally in 1997, despite lower non-recurring revenue and higher net lending, reflects a continued improvement in the underlying primary balance," the office said.
